title: Scandinavian Defense Dissected | Develop Your Instincts | GM Naroditsky's DYI Speedrun

moves.spoken: We play the Sicilian — c5.
White plays a knight to f3.
We play d6.
White plays d4 and we capture on d4.
White recaptures with the knight and we develop a knight to f6.
White plays a bishop to d3 — a move that's gotten more popular. Its point is to reserve c4 for a Maroczy-style clamp. We're not tied to the Najdorf; stay flexible.
The d4 knight is vulnerable, so we exploit it and develop at once — Rauzer style, the Classical Sicilian: a knight to c6.
A knight to c6, challenging the d4 knight and asking White a question.
White captures on c6 — but this trade is almost always good for Black in the Sicilian.
We recapture with the b-pawn, getting a very mobile pawn mass and the semi-open b-file.
White plays c4. Now we decide about our f8 bishop — as an experienced Sicilian player, we make the right call.
e5 and a bishop to e7 lack pizzazz — instead we play Dragon-style and fianchetto with g6.
White plays a knight to c3 — and I'm eyeing the weak dark squares.
We fianchetto with a bishop to g7.
Because White has committed to c4, this bishop's control of the long diagonal can never be blocked by a pawn — and in the long run I eye the b2 pawn.
We castle. We still have the light-squared bishop to develop, but no rush — let's see what White does.

White plays h3, a nonchalant move usually preparing a bishop to e3 while guarding against a knight to g4. The c4 pawn is a long-term target: a bishop to e6 or a6 is where it belongs, but we needn't commit yet.
So a rook to b8 onto the semi-open file — a low-risk improving move that pressures b2, and White's rook will be passive after a rook to b1.
White plays a queen to a4 — risky, since the queen is easily targeted. A knight to d7 comes to mind, eyeing c5; c6 isn't really hanging, as a queen grab drops to a knight to e5.
But we don't need tactics — a queen to c7 defends both pawns easily, and keeps the capture on b2 alive since the c3 knight is undermined.

White plays b4 — and we have a tactic. Not the automatic knight to d7: the money move is a knight capture on e4. After a bishop recaptures, we play a bishop capture on a1; if a bishop to h6, we drop back to g7.
We capture on e4. We're not afraid to give up the fianchettoed bishop, because we'll be up the exchange with White's queen far offside.
White recaptures on e4 — a move that should never be played automatically, with hidden dangers.
We capture on c3.
White plays a rook to b1. We're up a pawn, but c6 is hanging and we'd like to defend it.
A bishop to d7 defends and sets up discoveries against the queen — I don't mind trading the dark-squared bishops, since White has no kingside attack and our structure keeps the king safe.
White plays a3 — slow. d5 tempts, but it has a hidden defect: a queen to c2 sets up a capture on d5. So don't engage tactically yet.
We simply drop the bishop back to g7 — not glamorous, but it avoids complications and makes d5 a huge idea.
White plays a bishop to b2 — and trading bishops is fine; e5 setting up d5 is also excellent.
We trade on b2.
White recaptures, and now it's time for d5 — we shift focus to the center where our extra pawn lives and steamroll: not d4 first, but e5, then e4, f5, f4, f3.
White plays a bishop to d3, and we push e5.
e5 — we want to follow with e4.
White plays b5. Not a capture on b5, which the queen retakes — keep the central mass intact by not giving up d5.
We capture on b5, hitting the queen.
White recaptures. A queen to c3 tempts, but a rook to b3 defends both bishop and rook — unless we deflect the queen first.
So a6, deflecting the queen — a queen grab on a6 runs into a queen to c3 forking, and a6 also threatens a capture on b5. Probably the best move.
White plays a rook to b1, not biting.
Many roads lead to Rome — we capture on b5.
White recaptures on b5.
A bishop to f5, chasing a rook while keeping the bishop pinned to the other rook — don't over-simplify; the more you trade, the harder the win.
White plays a rook to d1. A queen to c3 tempts and might be crushing, but let's see.
A queen to c3 — after a rook to b3 we drop back threatening a bishop to c2.
I avoid the queen to c3 because of a queen to b4 trading into an undefended rook — so d4 for now, keeping options open.
d4 pushes the passer.
I like a check — or now a queen to c3 on a protected square, since the d-pawn guards the queen, so any queen trade forks the rooks.
The b2 rook is attacked twice and defended once, so we threaten a bishop to d7 — and, for extra credit, a bishop to d3 does the same via a second deflection.
White plays a queen to a6, wanting a4 to protect the bishop.
I combine ideas — e4, so that with d4 the idea is to push e3.
White plays a4.
We push e3 to win — huff and puff on White's position and something gives.
We recapture on e3 with the pawn, not forgetting our old ideas.
The old idea was to deflect the bishop.
So a great time for a bishop to d3.
White captures on d3.
And we win with a capture on b2 — if a rook to e3, the king is vulnerable, so look for forks.
After a rook capture on e3, a queen check on c1.
We take another rook — beautiful.
A queen to f6 — sometimes 1100s are damn good; what's the cleanest win?
White plays a rook to f2.
A queen to b2 is better than taking on d3 — go for mate or the queen trade.
A queen to d6 — if you can win the bishop, do it; winning material eases the task.
We win the bishop with a rook to d2 using another pin.
A queen capture on f8 with check — we take the bishop next.
The king recaptures on f8.
White plays a bishop to a6.
A queen to f3 is clinical, preventing a bishop to b7 — because there a rook capture on g2 and a queen to f1 is mate.
There a rook capture on g2 and a queen to f1 is mate.
Checkmate — a big round of applause to our opponent.

On the opening: a knight to c6 is the best move against a bishop to d3. That's the Rauzer — an underrated Sicilian. White's main try is a bishop to g5, and if White plays f4 like in the Najdorf, that's already bad here, because Black has h6 and a bishop to e7 and White can't play a queen to f3. Against a queen to d2, the knight-takes-e4 tactic wins a pawn, the same theme as the Najdorf. The whole line is a very similar shape to an Accelerated Dragon against the Maroczy: notice how our knight is a key piece, rerouting to c5 or d4 to clamp the weak dark squares. After a queen to a4, the engine move is a knight to d7, and after a queen grab on a7 the correct move is the surprising queen to b6 — Benko-Gambit style, where Black gets long-term queenside counterplay White can never solve, even with queens off, because the b2 pawn is a permanent problem. A key caution: be careful with the knight-takes-c4 tactic — it isn't always as good as it looks. In a 2014 King's Indian of mine, a similar knight-and-bishop grab on a1 backfired to a knight to b2 forcing the rook, then a bishop to h6 and a crushing kingside attack. It only worked for us here because we came out up the exchange with White's kingside bare.

One clarification: the real Maroczy Bind is a c4 response to the Accelerated Dragon — I was using the term informally for the e4-and-c4 pawns. Notice again how the knight, rerouting to c5 or d4, is what clamps the central dark squares — the main drawback of this White system.
